newsitem.title: FRANCE: Former BoF council member sees EMU start on time.
newsitem.headline: Former BoF council member sees EMU start on time.

text.p: Former Bank of France policy maker Jean Boissonnat said on Tuesday he was sure European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would be launched on time by a majority of European Union countries.

He said he believed all EU nations would be part of the euro from January 1, 2002 as long as the EU used the time between January 1, 1999 and 2002 -- when currency parities will be fixed but euro notes not yet in public circulation -- to help all countries meet Maastricht treaty criteria.

"I am firmly convinced the euro will exist at the date forecast by the Maastricht treaty," Boissonnat, whose term on the Bank of France Monetary Policy Council ended in January, told a business lunch.
"Only one thing can prevent it -- a recession in Europe in 1997 and there will be no such recession."

"Everybody will be there from 2002. No Frenchman will have a euro in his pocket without an Italian having one, too. No German will have euros in his pocket without the Portuguese having them," he said.
Boissonnat said it would be a bad idea to delay the fixing of parities in 1999 because the period between then and 2002 was a crucial period of adjustment.
"The euro must exist in 1999 so that we can all reach our objectives by 2002," he said. "The fuse will be lit in 1999 but the rocket will not take off until 2002."

The Maastricht treaty, which sets financial criteria for countries participating in EMU, left enough room for interpretation so that he could predict with confidence that it would be founded by a majority of European Union states.
"The presence of room for manoeuvre in the treaty is what allows me to say, a year ahead of time, that a majority of EU countries will qualify for the single currency on time."

He said the period between January 1999 and January 2002 should be used as a time for countries not quite ready for the 1999 deadline to improve their situation so they can participate in EMU three years later.

"We should not push Portugal, Spain and Italy to make efforts beyond what their populations can tolerate because they would then enter the euro wounded, which would be no good for them and no good for the rest of us," Boissonat said.
